scope: Offline educational fitness application for generally healthy adults

sources.title: A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate for population prediction; limited for an individual's true RMR
sources.summary: Researchers measured resting energy expenditure by indirect calorimetry in 498 healthy adults aged 19–78, including normal-weight and obese participants. Weight, height, age, and sex predicted resting expenditure with R²=0.71. The simplified equations preserved predictive performance. This is an estimate of resting expenditure, not total daily energy needs.
supportedClaims: Male equation: 10×kg + 6.25×cm − 5×years + 5 kcal/day.
Female equation: 10×kg + 6.25×cm − 5×years − 161 kcal/day.
limitations: Original binary sex categories are model coefficients, not a full representation of gender or physiology.
Activity multipliers and precise error intervals are not provided by this paper.
Not validated here for children, pregnancy, illness, or every athlete population.

sources.title: Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate for dynamic population modeling; individual forecasts remain uncertain
sources.summary: A physiological model accounts for changes in body composition and energy expenditure as weight changes. It explains why a constant calorie deficit does not produce unlimited linear weight loss. Resting expenditure and movement costs change with weight. Baseline energy requirements and adherence create substantial uncertainty in forecasts.
supportedClaims: The 3500-kcal-per-pound rule ignores adaptation and should not be extrapolated into long-term guaranteed weight loss.
Weight forecasts should account for changing expenditure.
limitations: A simple app calculation is not the validated full Hall model.
A 7700-kcal-per-kg conversion is only an energy-equivalent illustration, not a reliable timeline or tissue-composition prediction.

sources.title: Energy compensation and adiposity in humans
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate association evidence; insufficient for individual causal adjustment
sources.summary: An analysis of 1,754 adults with total and basal energy-expenditure data found evidence that activity expenditure and basal expenditure can compensate. The modeled average compensation was 28%, with substantial variation related to body composition. The observational design cannot resolve causal direction.
supportedClaims: Additional activity need not increase total daily expenditure by the full estimated exercise energy cost.
Compensation differs between individuals.
limitations: Do not automatically subtract 28% from a user's exercise calories.
This cross-sectional population association is not a personal exercise-response equation or proof of a causal mechanism.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.type: authoritative position stand / overview of reviews
sources.evidenceStrength: High for broad benefits; variable for specific programming comparisons
sources.summary: The updated ACSM position stand synthesized 137 reviews covering over 30,000 participants. Progressive resistance training improves strength, hypertrophy, and physical function. Strength can benefit from heavier loads, full range of motion, 2–3 sets, and at least two weekly sessions. Higher weekly volume can enhance hypertrophy. Failure training and complex programming did not consistently improve outcomes.
supportedClaims: Strength was enhanced with ≥80% 1RM loads and ≥2 sessions/week.
Hypertrophy was enhanced by ≥10 sets/week.
Progressive resistance training is recommended for healthy adults.
limitations: A volume threshold is not a universal optimal dose or minimum needed for any benefit.
Evidence varies by outcome; most interventions lasted 6–52 weeks.
This updates the 2009 position stand.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate historical guidance; superseded as general guidance by ACSM 2026
sources.summary: The earlier ACSM position stand described progressive overload and practical load progression. At a specified repetition-maximum load, it recommended increasing resistance by 2–10% when the trainee can exceed the target by one or two repetitions. Recommendations were to be tailored to goals, ability, and experience.
supportedClaims: A 2–10% load increase after exceeding the desired repetition target is an established historical progression approach.
limitations: This is a practical progression rule, not a proven universal optimum.
Use small feasible increments and user judgment; current general training guidance should cite ACSM 2026.
The original abstract does not specify a two-session confirmation.

sources.title: Novel Resistance Training-Specific Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale Measuring Repetitions in Reserve
sources.evidenceStrength: Limited-to-moderate for scale use
sources.summary: Twenty-nine novice and experienced squatters reported perceived exertion using a repetitions-in-reserve scale. Ratings were inversely associated with repetition velocity. The scale provides a practical way to report how many further repetitions a person believes they could complete and to adjust daily training effort.
supportedClaims: RPE 10 corresponds to 0 RIR; RPE 9 to 1 RIR; RPE 8 to 2 RIR.
limitations: RIR is subjective, not a direct measurement of remaining capability.
The small squat study does not establish exact accuracy across all exercises or users.
RPE-to-RIR mapping is a scale convention.

sources.title: Similar muscle hypertrophy following eight weeks of resistance training to momentary muscular failure or with repetitions-in-reserve in resistance-trained individuals
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate for the studied program; limited generalizability
sources.summary: Participants trained each leg with either failure sets or sets stopped at perceived 1–2 repetitions in reserve during an eight-week leg press and leg extension program. Overall quadriceps growth was similar. Failure training produced greater acute fatigue, supporting the feasibility of stopping slightly short of failure.
supportedClaims: In this study, 1–2 RIR produced similar overall quadriceps hypertrophy to failure training.
limitations: The finding concerns trained adults, two lower-body exercises, and eight weeks.
It does not prove that every RIR target is equivalent or establish an optimal RIR for all goals.

sources.title: Prediction of one repetition maximum strength from multiple repetition maximum testing and anthropometry
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate for studied exercises and repetition ranges
sources.summary: Seventy adults completed bench press and leg press maximum tests at 1, 5, 10, and 20 repetitions. The relationship between repetition count and load was nonlinear. Five-repetition tests produced the strongest predictions; accuracy declined at higher repetitions.
supportedClaims: For the studied bench press and leg press, no more than 10 repetitions should be used in linear 1RM estimates.
Prediction depends on the exercise and repetition range.
limitations: This study developed its own equations; it is not universal validation of Epley.
Restricting an app's Epley input to 2–10 repetitions is a conservative product choice informed by this evidence.

sources.title: Age-predicted maximal heart rate revisited
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate for population mean; limited individual precision
sources.summary: A meta-analysis and laboratory study of 514 healthy adults supported an age-based maximum-heart-rate prediction of 208 minus 0.7 times age. Individual values varied substantially, with laboratory standard deviations of 7–11 beats per minute. Age prediction provides a broad guide, not an individual's measured maximum.
supportedClaims: Estimated HRmax = 208 − 0.7×age in years.
Individual HRmax can differ meaningfully from age prediction.
limitations: Healthy, unmedicated, nonsmoking adults were studied.
Medication and cardiovascular conditions can affect heart rate.
An approximate ±10 bpm illustration is not a formal individual confidence interval.

sources.title: Target Heart Rates Chart
sources.evidenceStrength: Authoritative general guide; approximate intensity boundaries
sources.summary: The AHA describes moderate activity as roughly 50–70% of maximum heart rate and vigorous activity as roughly 70–85%. These are averages for general guidance. Medication and heart conditions may require different individualized targets.
supportedClaims: AHA moderate guide: 0.50–0.70×HRmax.
AHA vigorous guide: 0.70–0.85×HRmax.
limitations: The AHA page uses 220−age; applying its percentages to Tanaka HRmax combines two disclosed sources.
These percentages are not lactate or ventilatory threshold measurements.
Do not substitute these percentages for heart-rate-reserve percentages.

sources.title: 2024 Adult Compendium of Physical Activities: A third update of the energy costs of human activities
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate for standardized activity classification; limited for personal calories
sources.summary: The updated Adult Compendium standardizes the estimated energy cost of many activities using MET values. One standard MET uses a resting reference of 3.5 mL oxygen/kg/min. Values describe activity categories and help compare intensity; they do not measure the exact energy use of an individual session.
supportedClaims: Standard MET values can support broad exercise-energy estimates.
The general adult reference is intended for non-disabled adults without conditions materially affecting metabolism.
limitations: Efficiency, pace, terrain, and individual resting metabolism change true expenditure.
A MET estimate should not be presented as measured calories.
The Adult Compendium covers ages 19–59; separate references exist for older adults.

sources.title: Compendium of Physical Activities: definition of terms and corrected METs
sources.evidenceStrength: Strong for the reference convention; limited individual prediction
sources.summary: The Compendium defines one MET approximately as 1 kcal/kg/hour and explains that it was designed to standardize epidemiological activity classifications. Its authors state that it was not designed to determine precise individual activity energy costs. Standard METs do not correct for a person's age, sex, body size, or measured resting metabolism.
supportedClaims: Gross kcal ≈ MET×body mass in kg×duration in hours.
Subtracting one resting MET gives an approximate net increment above rest.
limitations: The net subtraction is arithmetic under the standard-MET assumption, not a validated personalized correction.
Gross calories include resting expenditure.
Do not automatically add activity estimates to a daily estimate that already includes that activity.

sources.title: How to Measure Physical Activity Intensity
authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.evidenceStrength: Authoritative general guidance
sources.summary: CDC distinguishes absolute activity intensity from intensity relative to the individual's fitness. Moderate aerobic activity generally permits talking but not singing. During vigorous activity, speaking more than a few words requires a breath. Absolute moderate intensity spans 3–5.9 METs; vigorous intensity begins at 6 METs.
supportedClaims: The talk test is a practical alternative or companion to heart-rate estimates.
Absolute intensity: 3–5.9 METs moderate; ≥6 METs vigorous.
limitations: Absolute MET categories do not necessarily match an individual's relative exertion.
Use relative effort when assessing whether an activity feels moderate or vigorous for the user.

sources.title: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
sources.evidenceStrength: Strong recommendation; moderate certainty for adult activity targets
sources.summary: For adults, WHO recommends 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity or 75–150 vigorous minutes weekly, or an equivalent mix, plus strengthening all major muscle groups on at least two days. Some activity is better than none. Starting with small amounts and building gradually provides benefit. Reducing sedentary time also matters.
supportedClaims: Adult weekly target: 150–300 moderate minutes or 75–150 vigorous minutes.
Muscle strengthening: ≥2 days/week.
A mixed-minute tally can treat one vigorous minute as two moderate-equivalent minutes.
limitations: These are public-health targets, not individualized performance prescriptions.
Adult recommendations should not be applied unchanged to children.
WHO 2020 adult guidelines do not provide an adult sleep-duration target.

sources.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society
sources.evidenceStrength: Consensus supported by evidence review; individual needs vary
sources.summary: The AASM and Sleep Research Society recommend that healthy adults aged 18–60 regularly sleep at least seven hours per night. Sleep need varies by individual and circumstances. More than nine hours may be appropriate during recovery from sleep debt, illness, or for young adults.
supportedClaims: Adults aged 18–60: aim for ≥7 hours of sleep regularly.
limitations: This is AASM/SRS guidance, not an adult WHO sleep recommendation.
Sleep duration alone does not fully describe sleep quality or recovery.
Do not treat eight hours as a guaranteed optimum for every adult.

sources.title: Body mass index as a measure of body fatness: age- and sex-specific prediction formulas
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate group prediction; limited individual precision
sources.summary: Body composition data from 1,229 people supported a BMI-, age-, and sex-based adult body-fat equation. Its standard error of estimate was 4.1 percentage points. The adult formula slightly overestimated body fat in obese participants. BMI-based body fat is an estimate and cannot directly distinguish muscularity from adiposity.
supportedClaims: Adult BF% = 1.20×BMI + 0.23×age − 10.8×sex − 5.4; male=1, female=0.
BMI = kg / metres².
Reported SEE = 4.1 body-fat percentage points.
limitations: SEE is not an individual's guaranteed error bound.
Binary sex coefficients and population sampling limit generalization.
Do not show an estimate as a measured body-fat value or use it to infer small tissue changes.

sources.title: Accuracy of Smart Scales on Weight and Body Composition: Observational Study
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate for tested devices and patient sample; limited generalizability
sources.summary: Three consumer smart scales were compared with DXA in hospital patients. Weight readings were reasonably accurate, while fat and lean-mass estimates had substantial disagreement. The authors advised against routinely using the devices for clinical body-composition assessment.
supportedClaims: A weight reading and a device's body-composition estimate have different accuracy.
Do not assume a precise-looking consumer body-fat percentage is a direct measurement.
limitations: Only three devices and a hospital population were studied.
The design did not establish within-person trend accuracy or performance of every newer device.
A single body-fat change does not establish fat or muscle gain/loss.

sources.title: The accuracy of prediction equations for estimating 1-RM performance in the bench press, squat, and deadlift
sources.evidenceStrength: Limited to moderate; college students, three lifts
sources.summary: Researchers compared seven published prediction equations against measured one-repetition maximum in the bench press, squat and deadlift in college students. The equations were reasonably accurate for the bench press and squat and underestimated the deadlift. The app uses the Epley form, load × (1 + reps/30), which first appeared in Boyd Epley's 1985 "Poundage chart" (Boyd Epley Workout, Body Enterprises, Lincoln, NE), not in this paper; this study supports the general usefulness of such equations, not Epley's formula specifically.
supportedClaims: Repetition-based equations such as Epley give a usable estimate of one-repetition maximum for the bench press and squat.
Estimated maximums are approximations and should be labelled as estimates.
limitations: Accuracy falls as reps rise above about 10.
Estimates are exercise-specific; the deadlift was underestimated.
Participants were college students, so results may not carry over to other groups.

sources.title: The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate to strong for population-level dose-response; individual response varies
sources.summary: Multilevel meta-regressions pooled 67 studies with 2,058 participants. Sets that only indirectly train a muscle were counted as 0.5 of a set ("fractional"), which had the strongest relative evidence of the counting methods tested. Muscle size and strength rose with weekly set volume, with diminishing returns that were more pronounced for strength. Frequency had effects on hypertrophy compatible with negligible, while strength gains rose with frequency, again with diminishing returns.
supportedClaims: Weekly sets per muscle show a dose-response with diminishing returns.
Counting secondary-muscle sets as half a set fits the data best.
Training frequency matters little for hypertrophy when volume is equal; it appears more relevant for strength.
limitations: Participants were mostly young men (79.1%), average age about 25.
Meta-regression shows associations across studies, not individual prescriptions.
The 0.5 weighting is a best-fitting convention, not a measured physiological constant.

sources.title: Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate; small number of studies
sources.summary: A meta-regression of 15 studies (34 treatment groups) found that more weekly sets were associated with greater muscle growth. Each additional weekly set was associated with a 0.37% larger percentage gain, and higher-volume groups gained about 3.9% more than lower-volume groups. The three-level comparison (under 5, 5–9 and 10+ sets per muscle) showed only a trend (P = 0.074). The authors describe a graded dose-response relationship.
supportedClaims: More weekly sets per muscle generally produce more growth, in a graded way.
limitations: Only 15 studies were included, and the three-level volume comparison was not statistically significant.
Does not show where returns level off for an individual.
Superseded in detail by newer dose-response work.

sources.title: Loading recommendations for muscle strength, hypertrophy, and local endurance: A re-examination of the repetition continuum
sources.evidenceStrength: Low to moderate; narrative review and author interpretation
sources.summary: This narrative review challenges the idea that each repetition range is tied to a specific adaptation. Based on emerging evidence, the authors propose that muscular adaptations, including hypertrophy, can be obtained across a wide spectrum of loading zones. The app uses it to support flexible rep ranges for growth. The abstract does not itself state the heavier-load advantage for maximal strength, which the app takes from the wider literature.
supportedClaims: Muscle growth is similar across a wide range of rep counts when sets are hard.
Heavier loads are better for maximal strength.
limitations: Narrative review without a formal pooled analysis.
The strength-specific claim and the condition that sets are hard are not stated in the abstract and were not verified against the full text.

sources.title: Influence of resistance training proximity-to-failure on skeletal muscle hypertrophy: A systematic review with meta-analysis
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate; 15 studies with varied failure definitions
sources.summary: A meta-analysis of 15 studies compared training to failure with stopping short. Using any definition of set failure there was a trivial advantage for failure (effect size 0.19, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.37). For momentary muscular failure specifically there was no clear advantage (effect size 0.12, CI -0.13 to 0.37). The authors conclude there is no evidence that training to momentary failure is superior for hypertrophy.
supportedClaims: Training to failure is not required for growth.
Stopping a few reps short gives similar growth.
limitations: Studies defined failure and non-failure differently.
Results concern hypertrophy, not strength or recovery cost.
A trivial benefit of set failure under the broad definition cannot be ruled out.

sources.title: Progressive overload without progressing load? The effects of load or repetition progression on muscular adaptations
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate to low; 43 participants, 8 weeks
sources.summary: Forty-three resistance-trained people were randomized to add load at a fixed rep range or add reps at a fixed load, training lower body twice a week for 8 weeks. Rectus femoris growth modestly favored adding reps and strength slightly favored adding load, both of questionable practical significance. Other outcomes were essentially the same. Both progression methods appear viable.
supportedClaims: Adding reps and adding load are both valid ways to progress.
Basis for double progression.
limitations: Short 8-week study in trained lifters, lower body only.
Small differences were uncertain with wide intervals.

sources.title: Gaining more from doing less? The effects of a one-week deload period during supervised resistance training on muscular adaptations
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate to low; 39 participants, single 9-week program
sources.summary: Thirty-nine resistance-trained adults were randomized to rest completely from lifting for one week at the midpoint of a 9-week high-volume program or to train continuously. Lower-body muscle size, endurance and power did not differ, while continuous training produced larger gains in isometric and dynamic lower-body strength. Continuous training also showed slight psychological benefits on a readiness questionnaire.
supportedClaims: A planned week off mid-program did not improve growth and slightly reduced lower-body strength gains.
Basis for suggesting recovery weeks only when progress stalls.
limitations: The deload was complete rest, not reduced training.
Short program; upper-body training was unsupervised.
Does not test deloads for people who are actually stalled or fatigued.

sources.title: Integrating deloading into strength and physique sports training programmes: An international Delphi consensus approach
sources.evidenceStrength: Low; expert opinion, not a trial
sources.summary: Expert strength and physique coaches rated statements about deloading across three Delphi rounds (34, 29 and 21 coaches completed rounds one to three). The panel reached consensus on design principles and proposed defining a deload as a period of reduced training stress meant to reduce fatigue, promote recovery and improve preparedness for later training. It reflects coaching practice rather than measured outcomes.
supportedClaims: Expert consensus describes deloads as a period of reduced training stress.
limitations: Consensus of coaches, not evidence that deloads improve results.
Small panel that shrank between rounds.

sources.title: Give it a rest: a systematic review with Bayesian meta-analysis on the effect of inter-set rest interval duration on muscle hypertrophy
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate to low; 9 studies, substantial heterogeneity
sources.summary: Nine randomized studies (19 measurements) compared different rest intervals between sets with other variables controlled. Results suggest a small hypertrophic benefit from resting longer than about 60 seconds, possibly through preserving volume load. No appreciable differences were detected when resting beyond about 90 seconds.
supportedClaims: Rest longer than about 60 s gives a small growth benefit.
Little is added beyond about 90 s.
limitations: Few studies and substantial heterogeneity.
Credible intervals included zero for the longer-versus-shorter comparisons.
Hypertrophy only, not strength or time efficiency.

sources.title: Efficacy of split versus full-body resistance training on strength and muscle growth: A systematic review with meta-analysis
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate; 14 studies, 392 participants
sources.summary: Fourteen studies with 392 participants compared split and full-body routines. Strength gains in the bench press and lower limbs, and muscle size measures including lean body mass, were not significantly different between routines when training volume was equated. The authors conclude people can choose a routine by preference.
supportedClaims: Split and full-body routines give similar results when weekly volume is equal.
limitations: Few studies per muscle outcome.
Only applies when volume is matched.

sources.title: What influence does resistance exercise order have on muscular strength gains and muscle hypertrophy? A systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate; 11 good-to-excellent quality studies
sources.summary: Eleven studies were pooled. Overall strength gains did not differ by order, but strength gains were larger in whichever exercise type was performed first (multi-joint first favored multi-joint strength, single-joint first favored single-joint strength). No significant effect of exercise order was found for hypertrophy.
supportedClaims: Exercises done first in a session gain more strength.
Order does not change muscle growth.
limitations: Few studies per comparison.
Short interventions, so long-term effects are unknown.

sources.title: Effect of free-weight vs. machine-based strength training on maximal strength, hypertrophy and jump performance - a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate; 13 studies, 1,016 participants, only 5 for hypertrophy
sources.summary: Thirteen studies with 1,016 adults were pooled. Hypertrophy and jump performance did not differ between free-weight and machine training. Strength gains were specific to the training type: free-weight tests improved more after free-weight training, with a similar tendency for machines.
supportedClaims: Free weights and machines build similar muscle.
Strength gains are largest in the type you train.
limitations: Only five studies measured hypertrophy.
Studies lasted at least 6 weeks and included adults aged 18 to 60 only.

sources.title: Low-load bench press and push-up induce similar muscle hypertrophy and strength gain
sources.evidenceStrength: Low; 18 young men, 8 weeks
sources.summary: Eighteen young men were randomized to bench press at 40% of their one-repetition maximum or push-ups adjusted (for example kneeling) to the same load, twice a week for 8 weeks. Both groups gained bench press strength and chest and triceps muscle thickness; biceps thickness rose only in the bench press group. The authors judged the two comparably effective.
supportedClaims: Push-ups and low-load bench press produced similar growth and strength gain.
limitations: Very small sample of young men.
Push-up position was adjusted to match a low load, so findings may not apply to standard push-ups.

sources.title: Greater hamstrings muscle hypertrophy but similar damage protection after training at long versus short muscle lengths
sources.evidenceStrength: Low to moderate; 20 adults, 12 weeks
sources.summary: Twenty healthy adults trained one leg with seated leg curls and the other with prone curls for 12 weeks, with muscle volume measured by MRI. Whole hamstring volume rose about 14% with seated curls versus 9% with prone curls, a difference seen in the biarticular but not the monoarticular hamstrings. Protection against later muscle damage was similar for both.
supportedClaims: Seated leg curls (hamstrings trained at long length) grew the hamstrings more than lying curls.
limitations: Small sample of healthy adults.
Only one exercise comparison per muscle.

sources.title: Triceps brachii hypertrophy is substantially greater after elbow extension training performed in the overhead versus neutral arm position
sources.evidenceStrength: Low to moderate; 21 adults, 12 weeks
sources.summary: Twenty-one adults did cable elbow extensions with one arm overhead and the other arm at the side for 12 weeks. MRI showed whole triceps volume rose about 19.9% overhead versus 13.9% at the side, and the long head about 28.5% versus 19.6%, despite lighter loads overhead.
supportedClaims: Overhead triceps extensions grew the triceps, especially the long head, more than the same exercise with the arm by the side.
limitations: Small sample.
Cable extension only; other triceps exercises were not tested.

sources.title: Triceps surae muscle hypertrophy is greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training
sources.evidenceStrength: Low; 14 untrained adults, 12 weeks
sources.summary: Fourteen untrained adults trained one leg with standing calf raises and the other with seated calf raises for 12 weeks. Gastrocnemius growth was far greater standing (lateral 12.4% vs 1.7%, medial 9.2% vs 0.6%), while soleus growth was similar (2.1% vs 2.9%).
supportedClaims: Standing calf raises grew the gastrocnemius far more than seated raises; soleus growth was similar.
limitations: Small sample of untrained adults.
Does not show whether seated raises add anything for the soleus in trained lifters.

sources.title: Hip thrust and back squat training elicit similar gluteus muscle hypertrophy and transfer similarly to the deadlift
sources.evidenceStrength: Low to moderate; 34 untrained adults, 9 weeks
sources.summary: Thirty-four untrained college-aged adults were randomized to hip thrust (18) or back squat (16) with equated set volume for 9 weeks. Gluteus growth was similar, with wide uncertainty. Squats produced greater growth in the quadriceps and adductors, and strength gains favored the trained lift. Deadlift strength improved similarly in both groups.
supportedClaims: Hip thrusts and squats grew the glutes similarly.
Squats grew the thighs more.
limitations: Untrained participants and a short 9-week period.
Wide confidence intervals for gluteal differences.

sources.title: Interpreting signal amplitudes in surface electromyography studies in sport and rehabilitation sciences
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate for methodological reasoning; not an outcome trial
sources.summary: This review explains what can and cannot be inferred from comparing surface EMG amplitudes between muscles, exercises and loads. The authors argue that conclusions about strength and hypertrophy drawn from such comparisons are frequently unsubstantiated and unwarranted.
supportedClaims: EMG amplitude cannot be used to rank exercises for growth.
Why the app describes muscle roles qualitatively rather than with percentages.
limitations: Does not test any training outcome directly.
Does not say which exercises are best.

sources.title: Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate to strong; 138 studies, N = 19,951, across many goal types
sources.summary: A meta-analysis of 138 randomized studies found interventions increased how often people monitored goal progress and modestly improved goal attainment (d = 0.40). Effects were larger when progress was physically recorded or reported publicly.
supportedClaims: Monitoring progress makes reaching a goal more likely, more so when progress is recorded.
limitations: Covers many kinds of goals, not specifically exercise.
Effect size is modest.

sources.title: The (over)use of SMART goals for physical activity promotion: A narrative review and critique
sources.evidenceStrength: Low to moderate; critical review, not a trial
sources.summary: This review examines the SMART goal acronym in physical activity promotion and argues it is not grounded in scientific theory, is not consistent with empirical evidence, and is applied inconsistently. It also notes a risk of harmful effects and offers recommendations for better goal-setting practice.
supportedClaims: SMART goals are not a proven standard, so the app avoids presenting them as such.
limitations: Critique rather than a test of alternatives.
Does not provide a replacement goal-setting method.

sources.title: Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation
sources.evidenceStrength: Low to moderate; expert review for a specialized population
sources.summary: This review of the literature on contest preparation recommends setting calories to produce bodyweight loss of roughly 0.5 to 1% per week to maximize muscle retention. It also covers protein, fat, meal timing and supplements for natural bodybuilders.
supportedClaims: Losing about 0.5–1% of body weight per week helps retain muscle.
limitations: Written for competitive natural bodybuilders; general applicability is assumed, not tested.
Narrative review, not a controlled trial.

sources.title: Nutrition recommendations for bodybuilders in the off-season: A narrative review
sources.evidenceStrength: Low to moderate; expert review for a specialized population
sources.summary: This narrative review recommends a modest calorie surplus (about 10 to 20%) with a target weight gain of roughly 0.25 to 0.5% of bodyweight per week for novice and intermediate bodybuilders. Advanced lifters are advised to be more conservative.
supportedClaims: Gaining about 0.25–0.5% of body weight per week for novice and intermediate lifters.
limitations: Written for natural bodybuilders; not a controlled trial.
Advanced lifters need smaller surpluses than the headline range.

sources.title: Energy deficiency impairs resistance training gains in lean mass but not strength: A meta-analysis and meta-regression
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate; pooled controlled trials, estimated threshold
sources.summary: Across trials of resistance training, people in an energy deficit gained less lean mass than people who were not, while strength gains were similar. The meta-regression estimated that a deficit of roughly 500 kcal a day was enough to stop lean-mass gains on average.
supportedClaims: Energy deficits larger than about 500 kcal/day tend to prevent lean-mass gains during resistance training.
limitations: The 500 kcal figure is a modelled average with uncertainty, not an individual limit.
Trials varied in diet control, training and participants.

sources.title: Effect of Small and Large Energy Surpluses on Strength, Muscle, and Skinfold Thickness in Resistance-Trained Individuals: A Parallel Groups Design
sources.evidenceStrength: Low to moderate; one trial in trained lifters
sources.summary: Trained lifters eating about 5% or about 15% above maintenance for eight weeks gained similar strength and muscle thickness, but the larger surplus added more skinfold thickness (fat).
supportedClaims: For trained lifters, a small surplus (about 5%) builds muscle about as well as a larger one, with less fat gain.
limitations: Small sample over eight weeks.
Surpluses were estimated, not measured.

sources.title: Long-term time-course of strength adaptation to minimal dose resistance training through retrospective longitudinal growth modeling
sources.evidenceStrength: Low to moderate; large sample but not randomized, minimal-dose training
sources.summary: Training records from 14,690 participants (60% female, mean age 48) doing once-weekly single sets to failure across six exercises were modeled for up to about 6.8 years. Strength followed a linear-log curve that approached a plateau by roughly 1 to 2 years, with about 30–50% gains in the first year and about 50–60% over baseline after six years.
supportedClaims: Strength follows a fast-then-plateau (roughly logarithmic) curve over years.
Why goal projections include a slowing scenario.
limitations: Retrospective data from a private exercise company.
Minimal-dose training in middle-aged adults may not match other programs.
The authors note it is unclear whether the plateau can be overcome with other approaches.

sources.title: Athletic records and human endurance
sources.evidenceStrength: Low to moderate; old analysis of record performances
sources.summary: Riegel analyzed athletic record performances across distances to describe how endurance falls as distance increases. The app uses the resulting power-law form, T2 = T1 × (D2/D1)^1.06, to predict race times from a known performance. The formula is an empirical fit to record-level data.
supportedClaims: Race-time prediction T2 = T1 × (D2/D1)^1.06.
limitations: Unreliable for much longer distances than the one measured.
Fitted to record performances, so less accurate for recreational runners.
Summary written from the abstract-level description; full text not reviewed.

sources.title: A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate; 49 randomized trials, 1,863 participants
sources.summary: Pooled 49 randomized trials of protein supplementation during resistance training in healthy adults. Extra protein added a small amount of fat-free mass and strength. In a meta-regression, gains in fat-free mass stopped increasing at a total daily intake of about 1.62 g per kg of body weight, with a 95% confidence interval of roughly 1.03 to 2.20 g/kg.
supportedClaims: About 1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight per day is a reasonable daily target for people who lift; more than that did not add measurable muscle on average.
limitations: The breakpoint has a wide confidence interval; some people may benefit from more.
Trials studied healthy adults; it does not apply to kidney disease or other medical conditions.
Supplementation trials, not whole-diet feeding studies.

sources.title: Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations Between Low- vs. High-Load Resistance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate; pooled randomized trials, mostly untrained participants
sources.summary: Twenty-one studies compared training with heavy loads (above 60% of a one-rep max) and light loads (60% or less), with sets taken to failure. Muscle growth was similar between the two. Gains in one-rep-max strength were greater with heavy loads. The app uses this to let people choose a lower or higher rep range for muscle growth, while keeping heavy main lifts heavy for strength.
supportedClaims: Muscle growth is similar with heavy and light loads when sets are taken to failure.
Heavier loads improve maximal strength more.
limitations: Most included studies had sets taken to failure; results may differ when sets stop further from failure.
Many studies used untrained participants and short interventions.

sources.title: Neither load nor systemic hormones determine resistance training-mediated hypertrophy or strength gains in resistance-trained young men
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate for trained young men; single trial
sources.summary: Forty-nine resistance-trained young men trained for 12 weeks with either 20–25 reps per set at a light load or 8–12 reps at a heavier load, all to failure. Muscle growth and most strength gains were similar; bench-press one-rep max improved somewhat more with the heavier load.
supportedClaims: Trained lifters grew as much from sets of 20–25 as from sets of 8–12 when sets were taken to failure.
limitations: Young trained men only.
Sets were taken to failure; the app's targets usually stop 1–3 reps short.

sources.title: Resistance Training Load Effects on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain: Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate; network meta-analysis of randomized trials
sources.summary: Randomized trials comparing low (15 or more reps), moderate (9–15) and high loads (8 or fewer) in healthy adults were pooled. Muscle growth was similar across load ranges when sets were performed to failure. Strength gains were greater with heavier loads.
supportedClaims: Muscle growth is similar across low, moderate and high loads when sets are taken to failure.
Heavier loads build maximal strength more.
limitations: Few trials directly compared every pair of load ranges.
Short interventions; results rely on sets to or near failure.

sources.title: Resistance training prescription for muscle strength and hypertrophy in healthy adults: a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis
sources.type: systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis
sources.evidenceStrength: Moderate to high; 192 randomized trials, 5,000+ participants
sources.summary: A large network meta-analysis of randomized trials compared training prescriptions. Almost any resistance training built muscle and strength. Strength gains were greatest with higher loads, ideally across multiple sets. Muscle growth was similar across a wide range of loads and set schemes.
supportedClaims: Muscle growth is similar across a wide range of loads.
Higher loads give the largest gains in maximal strength.
limitations: Network comparisons are partly indirect.
Healthy adults only; individual responses vary.

sources.title: Effects of different intensities of resistance training with equated volume load on muscle strength and hypertrophy
sources.evidenceStrength: Low to moderate; small single trial
sources.summary: Untrained men trained one limb at 20% of their one-rep max and the other at 40%, 60% or 80%, to failure, for 12 weeks. Loads of 40–80% produced similar muscle growth, but 20% produced clearly less. The app therefore keeps its 'higher reps' ranges to about 30 reps or fewer, which corresponds to loads above roughly 30–40% of a one-rep max.
supportedClaims: Very light loads around 20% of a one-rep max grow muscle less than 40–80%.
limitations: Small sample of untrained young men.
The exact lowest effective load is not established.

implementationNotes.note: Always label predicted RMR, TDEE, exercise energy, estimated 1RM, HRmax, and body-fat results as estimates. Do not imply a formula calculates a user's actual physiological value.
Mifflin estimates resting expenditure. An activity multiplier is an app starting assumption, not part of the Mifflin validation. Show the chosen multiplier and avoid double counting planned exercise.

Use consistently collected weight and intake trends to inform adjustments. A 14–28 day review window, a 7-day mean, or ±100–200 kcal changes are practical defaults, not thresholds validated by these papers.

Use same-unit load×(1+reps/30) for 2–10 near-maximal repetitions. For one completed maximal repetition, report the lifted load directly as a measured single. Do not automatically add RIR to reps without labeling that extrapolation as heuristic. Do not convert an estimate into an instruction to attempt a maximum.

A beginner can benefit from low volume. A starting 6–10 hard sets per muscle per week is a programming default; ≥10 is an evidence-supported hypertrophy-oriented target, not a prerequisite. Indirect-set counting and deload triggers are modeling conventions and should be disclosed.

Prefer moderate/vigorous bands and the talk test. If five zones are shown, label boundaries as a selectable coaching convention. Percent HRmax and percent heart-rate reserve are distinct methods and must not be mixed. Estimated bands do not locate physiological thresholds.

Do not assign health or attractiveness categories to a body-fat estimate. Keep device/manual readings separate from calculated estimates. No original Navy circumference report was directly verified in this research pass.
A readiness score derived from sleep, soreness, stress, and performance is an app heuristic. Show its components and permit user judgment; it is not a validated medical or overtraining diagnosis.

Muscle growth is similar across roughly 5–30 reps per set when sets end close to failure, so a lower or higher rep preference is offered for growth. Exact ranges per exercise kind, the 25–30 rep ceiling, the extra rest for heavy sets and keeping heavy main lifts unchanged are app conventions informed by these papers, not values the papers prescribe.
